candidates.original_title: Biased attention and dysphoria: Manipulating selective attention reduces subsequent depressive symptoms
candidates.description: Attentional retraining reduces depressive symptoms through changes in attentional bias in dysphoric individuals
candidates.citation_sentence: The current study replicated Wells and Beevers' (2010) findings on re-training the negative attentional bias in dysphoric individuals.
candidates.notes: Single replication study; authors explicitly state failure in Discussion: 'The replication was not successful' and 'attention was not found to be related to a change in mood.'

candidates.original_title: Biased attention and dysphoria: Manipulating selective attention reduces subsequent depressive symptoms
candidates.description: Attentional retraining toward neutral stimuli reduces depressive symptoms in dysphoric individuals, relative to a no-training condition.
candidates.citation_sentence: The current study replicated Wells and Beevers' (2010) findings on re-training the negative attentional bias in dysphoric individuals.
candidates.notes: Both training and no-training groups showed reductions in depressive symptoms, with no significant group difference or time-by-group interaction; the paper explicitly describes this as a failure to replicate.

candidates.original_title: Biased attention and dysphoria: Manipulating selective attention reduces subsequent depressive symptoms
candidates.description: Attentional retraining toward neutral stimuli reduces negative attentional bias in dysphoric individuals.
candidates.citation_sentence: The current study replicated Wells and Beevers' (2010) findings on re-training the negative attentional bias in dysphoric individuals.
candidates.notes: The replication found no significant time-by-training-condition interaction for attentional bias and explicitly stated that the expected change was not observed. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
